resources.string: Follicular cells line the colloid-filled lumen. Thyroglobulin is stored in the colloid.
TSH acts at the basal side; thyroid hormones are released toward the surrounding microvasculature.
This illustrated C cell lies near the follicular epithelium and does not open into the colloid.
C cells secrete calcitonin, not the T3 and T4 made by follicular cells.
Chief cells sense extracellular calcium. Lower calcium generally stimulates PTH release.
The hormone enters the local circulation and participates in systemic calcium regulation.
The illustrated zona fasciculata cell stores cholesterol esters that can support steroid synthesis.
Mitochondria carry out some steps of steroid synthesis; different cortex zones have distinct roles.
Preganglionic sympathetic input activates chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla.
Dense granules store catecholamines such as epinephrine or norepinephrine before release to blood.
Growth hormone supports growth and metabolism directly and through signals such as IGF-1.
This diagram identifies the cell by its secretion, not by shape or color in a tissue sample.
Prolactin supports milk production, distinct from oxytocin-mediated milk ejection.
This diagram identifies the cell by its secretion, not by shape or color in a tissue sample.
ACTH stimulates cortisol production in the adrenal cortex. It is not the nerve signal to the adrenal medulla.
This diagram identifies the cell by its secretion, not by shape or color in a tissue sample.
TSH stimulates thyroid follicular cells. Thyroid hormone feedback helps restrain its release.
This diagram identifies the cell by its secretion, not by shape or color in a tissue sample.
Gonadotrophs release LH and FSH in response to hypothalamic signals.
This diagram identifies the cell by its secretion, not by shape or color in a tissue sample.
Pinealocytes have processes that extend through the gland. Melatonin is a night-related signal, not a measurement from this drawing.
Pinealocytes are the main melatonin-producing cells in the pineal gland.
Leydig cells sit between seminiferous tubules, outside the epithelium that supports sperm development.
Leydig cells use cholesterol-derived substrates to produce testosterone, in response to LH.
Granulosa cells line the follicular compartment and surround and support the oocyte.
This oocyte is shown only for spatial context; it is not a granulosa cell.
The theca surrounds the granulosa layer. This highlighted example represents the steroid-producing inner thecal layer.
The theca lies on the vascular side of the follicular basement membrane; the granulosa and its lumen are inside.
Thyroglobulin is stored in this follicular compartment. The identity of the colloid is separate from blood thyroid hormone levels.
Parathyroid glands commonly lie on the posterior aspect of the thyroid; their locations can vary.
The posterior view shows the usual four-gland arrangement. These are not parts of the thyroid hormone pathway.
The gland is surrounded by a connective tissue capsule.
Cortical zones produce different steroid hormones; the highlighted area is part of the cortex.
The central medulla contains chromaffin cells. It is distinct from the steroid-producing cortex.
The glandular anterior lobe makes hormones such as ACTH, TSH and prolactin.
This lobe releases oxytocin and vasopressin synthesized in the hypothalamus; it does not make them.
The stalk connects the gland to the hypothalamus, carrying blood vessels and nerve fibers.
Secretory cell schematic, not diagnostic staining
Reduction from the initial signal: %1$s percentage points
Steady output = initial signal ÷ (1 + feedback strength).
This is a dimensionless example of linear negative feedback. The values are not hormone results, reference ranges or predictions.
T3 and T4 feed back on both the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. Calcitonin from C cells is separate.
This example shows how calcium regulation works without predicting calcium or PTH concentrations.
ACTH-driven cortisol release and sympathetic activation of the medulla are separate. The cortex example does not cover every cortical hormone.
The anterior lobe makes its own hormones. The posterior lobe releases hormones made by hypothalamic neurons.
